opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one of the areas where we're still very much at the beginning.

Right now the action space in Genie 3 is fairly constrained. The model is really good at what you might call navigation-style control: moving forward, turning, looking around, the kinds of inputs you'd have with a keyboard and mouse or a game controller. That's what makes the interactive, real-time experience feel compelling. You can walk through a world, and it stays consistent and responds to you.

But when you think about agents, you quickly want much richer interaction. You want an agent to pick something up, open a door, use a tool, manipulate objects in fine-grained ways, or interact with other agents in the scene. Many of those interactions aren't directly part of the agent's action space today. Some of that richness comes through what we call promptable world events, where you change the world with text, like "make it rain" or "add a character." That's powerful, but it's a different thing from the agent itself taking a precise, low-level action and seeing the physical consequences.

So I think of it as a few separate limitations. One is breadth: how many kinds of actions the model understands. Another is precision: whether an action produces exactly the consequence you'd expect, consistently, so an agent can actually learn from it. A third is that multi-agent interaction is still hard. Modeling several independent actors who affect each other in a coherent way is a much harder problem than modeling one camera moving through a world.

And there's duration. We can keep worlds consistent for a few minutes, which is a big step, but many interesting agent tasks need longer horizons.

That said, I'm optimistic. A lot of these capabilities seem to improve with scale and better data, and we've already seen the model learn surprising things about physics and consistency without anything explicit built in. Expanding the action space so an agent can really act in these worlds, rather than just move through them, is one of the most important directions for making world models useful for training embodied agents.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes text-driven world changes such as “make it rain” from precise actions performed by the agent.

r002.rationale: It does not explain how defining actions becomes harder when physical embodiment is replaced by visual pixels.

r003.rationale: It mentions opening a door as an example, but does not describe it as a sequence of physical micro-actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a fair question, and I think it's important to be honest about where things are. Right now, the action space in Genie 3 is fairly constrained. You have navigation actions, so moving around, looking around, the kinds of controls you'd expect from a first-person or third-person game environment. And then we have what we call promptable world events, where you can inject a text instruction and the world will respond to it, say, by making it rain, or having a character walk into the scene. But that's not the same thing as an agent having a rich, embodied action space where it can pick things up, manipulate objects, open doors, all of that.

So if you think about what an agent would need to actually learn complex behavior in a simulated world, the gap is really in that interaction layer. Navigation is a good start, and it's actually enough for a surprising number of tasks. You can test whether an agent can find its way to a goal, whether it can avoid obstacles, whether it generalizes to environments it's never seen. We did some early experiments with SIMA along those lines. But the moment you want to do something like, "go find the key and use it to unlock the door," you're pushing beyond what the native controls support.

Part of why it's limited is just the nature of how the model is trained. Genie learns from video, and the actions it understands are the ones it can infer as latent structure across a lot of footage. Locomotion and camera movement show up everywhere, so the model gets good at them. Fine-grained manipulation is much sparser and more varied, and it's harder to disentangle from the visual stream. So it's not a design choice so much as a reflection of what's learnable from the data we have today.

The other limitation I'd point to is the horizon. The world stays consistent for a few minutes now, which is a big improvement, but if you're running an agent for a very long episode, drift becomes an issue. For a lot of agent training you want to be able to run thousands of steps and trust that the environment hasn't quietly changed the rules on you.

So I'd summarize it as: the action space today is good enough to be useful for navigation-style tasks and for evaluating generalization, and the promptable events give you a kind of indirect, high-level control. But the direction we want to go is a much richer, more granular interface, where the agent's actions are closer to what a human could do in that world. That's an open research problem, and it's one of the things I'm most excited about working on next.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes navigation and manipulation performed by an agent from promptable events that change the world, such as making it rain or adding a character.

r002.rationale: It says fine-grained manipulation is harder to disentangle from video, but does not explain that defining actions becomes harder when physical embodiment is replaced by visual pixels alone.

r003.rationale: Opening doors is mentioned as an unsupported capability, but the response does not describe it as a sequence of physical micro-actions.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to separate what an agent can express through the interface from what the world model can reliably simulate. The action space is the first constraint: if an agent can only move and look around, then there are many tasks it simply can’t attempt. Navigating to an object is different from being able to pick it up, use it, or manipulate it precisely.

But exposing more actions doesn’t automatically solve that. The model also has to produce consistent consequences for those actions. Something can look plausible visually without being reliable enough for an agent to learn a useful behavior from it.

So I would think about the limitation in terms of the task. What actions does the agent need, and how faithfully does the environment respond to them? A rich visual world can be useful for some kinds of agent evaluation, but that alone doesn’t make it a general-purpose environment for every kind of interaction.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes available agent actions from how the world responds, but does not explain that controlling or prompting a world event may leave unspecified what action the agent performed.

r002.rationale: It discusses a visual world and limited actions, but does not say that defining agent actions becomes harder when physical embodiment is replaced by visual pixels.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention opening a door or describe it as a sequence of physical micro-actions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate the richness of the world from the richness of the actions an agent can take in it. A world can look very diverse, but that doesn’t mean the agent has an equally diverse set of ways to interact with it.

For Genie 3, you should think of the action space as constrained. Being able to navigate an environment and influence what happens is useful, but it doesn’t automatically give you arbitrary manipulation, precise control of every object, or the actions you would need for a particular robot.

So the question is really whether the actions available in the model match the task you want to train an agent on. And then there’s a separate question: does the world respond to those actions consistently enough that the agent learns something useful? Visual realism alone doesn’t establish that. You need to evaluate the interaction and, ultimately, whether what the agent learns transfers to the environment you care about.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes world richness from available actions, but does not explain that prompting a world event may fail to specify an action the agent itself performs.

r002.rationale: It mentions precise object control and robot-specific actions, but does not say that defining actions becomes harder when physical embodiment is replaced by visual pixels alone.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention opening a door or describe an action as a sequence of physical micro-actions.
